question.text: Suresh invests Rs.5,000 per month at 12% per annum from age 25 to age 35 (10 years) and then stops. He leaves the corpus invested until age 60. His friend Ramesh starts investing Rs.5,000 per month at age 35 and continues until age 60 (25 years) at the same rate. Who will have a larger corpus at age 60?

answer.text: Ramesh, because he invested for a longer period
Both will have approximately the same corpus
Suresh, because his money had more time to compound
Cannot be determined without knowing the exact rate

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the NISM Series XVII Retirement Adviser workbook (page 26), an early-starting investor ends with a larger corpus despite contributing for fewer years, and page 27 explains that a delayed saver loses the compounding benefit of the early years. Applying this to the stem at 12% annual, end-of-month contributions: Suresh's monthly Rs.5,000 from age 25-35 (left invested to 60) grows to roughly Rs.2.28 crore, while Ramesh's monthly Rs.5,000 from age 35-60 reaches only about Rs.93.94 lakh, so Suresh's corpus is larger. The Trap: Option A is the intuitive but wrong answer - longer contribution period does not compensate for the lost compounding years that Suresh enjoys. Note: The workbook's own illustration is at 8% (the X/Y example on page 26); the 12% recalculation above keeps the stem intact while remaining mathematically consistent.
